strengths: The paper identifies a useful problem: explaining predictions through interpretable macro-level attributes when omitted attributes can induce confounding. This has an identifiable audience in causal discovery, explainability, and model auditing.

PAGs and FCI provide an appropriate framework for representing latent confounding and partial identification under the stated assumptions. The background constraint that predictions cannot cause the attributes of their input images is well motivated.

The exposition clearly motivates population-level causal explanations and acknowledges limitations involving faithfulness, background knowledge, and feature selection. The synthetic example and two annotated image applications make the proposed workflow concrete.
weaknesses: Necessary—correct the interpretation of the empirical graphs. Section VI-C pools definite and possible causal edges into one stability score, although a stable circle-arrow edge remains compatible with a wholly confounded relationship. Conversely, absence of adjacency does not exclude an indirect causal effect. Figure 10, for example, permits a path from Cardiomegaly through Atelectasis to the prediction despite Cardiomegaly receiving zero adjacency stability. Report definite and possible ancestry separately and narrow claims that particular attributes are causally important or irrelevant.

Necessary—repair Example 1 and its appendix. The purported valid causal calculation uses marginal input-replacement expectations: for example, its coalition term for Z2 holds Z1's distribution unchanged despite Z2 causing Z1 in the stated SCM. The omitted-Z3 calculation then leaves Z3 fixed rather than integrating it through the observed-data distribution, so it does not represent the advertised adjustment using only Z2. Define the intervention and attribution estimands consistently and rederive the comparison. A zero attribution for one instance also does not, by itself, imply absence of population-level causal relevance.

Necessary—substantiate the statistical reliability of the learned PAGs. Conditional chi-square tests involving several categorical bird attributes can produce very sparse contingency tables; the X-ray analysis has only 239 observations and potentially rare findings. The manuscript does not establish test validity or robustness to the significance thresholds and conditioning-set restriction. Bootstrap edge stability can reproduce systematic testing errors. Provide appropriate diagnostics and sensitivity evidence, or present these outputs as exploratory hypotheses rather than validated causal explanations.

Necessary—address selection in the X-ray experiment. Controls are selected specifically for having 'no findings,' while the explanatory variables are findings and cases are selected for pneumonia. This makes inclusion depend on diagnosis and explanatory attributes. Section III dismisses selection bias as irrelevant, but robustness to latent confounding alone does not justify causal interpretation under this sampling scheme. Explain how selection affects the assumed graph and adjust the analysis or its claims accordingly.

Necessary—verify the synthetic predictor's claimed causal ground truth. Section V asserts that inspecting logistic-regression coefficients establishes dependence only on horizontal and vertical bars, but those coefficients are not supplied. Moreover, the regression consumes learned detector outputs, whose responses can themselves depend on other image content; detector accuracy does not establish causal invariance. An exactly specified prediction mechanism or controlled shape interventions on the complete predictor would substantiate the claimed causal versus confounded distinction.

Necessary—resolve contradictions that impede interpretation and reproduction. Figure 8 and Section VI-C identify Size, Eye Color, and Bill Shape as most stable, whereas Figure 9 names Wing Shape and Wing Pattern; Section VI-D's preference for Tail Shape over Tail Pattern also conflicts with Figure 8. The stated bird splits total 3,898 rather than 3,538 images, and 74.55% accuracy needs reconciliation with the stated 50-image X-ray test set. Specify which observations supply the predictions used for causal discovery and whether X-ray partitions separate patients.

Optional—a comparison against association-based rankings or causally sufficient discovery using the same annotations would help isolate the benefit of accommodating latent confounding. The LIME/SHAP illustrations primarily demonstrate differences in explanatory units and local versus population-level scope, rather than comparative causal accuracy.
